notes: Topology: a live map of clusters, servers, applications and the links between them, narrowed to what each person may see, with a full-window view.
Agents can ask for a scope they are missing, and every destructive call waits for a person to approve it, naming the application, key or cluster.
The first install is harder to get wrong: flui vault init opens the vault, provider tokens are asked without echo and checked, and --fits lists only sizes that suit Flui.
New installations: Loki caps the write-ahead log it replays on a restart, so a restart cannot loop on out-of-memory.
The public demo is read-only: visitors look around a real Flui and every invitation to sign in now points to installing Flui on your own server.

flui env create runs on a caller-supplied profile key (FLUI_PROFILE_KEY) without a vault, and creates no SSH certificate authority in ephemeral-key mode: the guided installer at app.flui.cloud can build installations again.

The dashboard holds far more visitors: metrics are cached briefly, Kubernetes connections are reused, application reads skip their history, access is remembered for two seconds and certificate checks are throttled.
The API can run as several autoscaled copies: background work runs once, long jobs finish before a copy stops, and the API and Postgres get more CPU.
Every server and server type shows its CPU architecture; arm servers come with a warning that apps deployed from a repository are built for x86.
An update also brings forward a master manifest whose ingress TLS binding the install record never noted, when the binding is proven on the master.
An update brings a master's templated manifests forward even when earlier updates left them from different releases: recorded values are proven against every release the files may come from.
flui env install-values adds the values an existing install record lacks, never changing a recorded one, so an update can bring the API manifest forward on installations whose record was incomplete.
The API also reads the sensitive variables set on the flui-api application, so secrets such as the Turnstile key set from the dashboard reach it.
The live activity demo fits a demo guest's area: it now asks for 225m of CPU and at most 1 CPU per component.
Demo sign-in lists both exact redirect URIs for GitHub as well as Google.
Every control node is an end of the Flui network: the API reaches clusters on other providers from any node, with promotion to the private address checked from every node.
Emergency switch back to the public address for a cluster on the Flui network: flui env overlay demote, and on the dashboard.
A master manifest pinned to a development build is read correctly again and moves to the release, so updates verify.
Sign-in pages and emails show Flui instead of Zitadel, with corrected Italian labels.
Self-registration closes again when the demo is switched off.
A platform update started with the bootstrap key backs up as the backup's owner instead of failing.
Account page: a QR code to add the authenticator app, drawn in the browser.
After signing out, the sign-in page offers a button instead of hanging on the redirect.
Demo visitors look around without signing up, connect their agent read-only, and keep their visit when they sign in to deploy.
Sign-in emails from the identity provider (verification, password reset) are sent through Flui's transactional mail.
The identity provider console is closed by default; an owner opens it for a limited time with flui identity console open.
Account page in Flui: profile, password, second factor and linked sign-ins, without the identity provider console.
Demo sign-in with GitHub and Google, and the guided GitHub App under an organisation.
The Flui registry can be switched on after install.
Platform addresses can be chosen, renamed and checked before they are created.
Networks are created in the requested zone, and clusters refuse a network that cannot reach their region.

Move an application and its PostgreSQL to a cluster at another provider with `flui migrate full`: a physical copy over a private link, a bridge that keeps the old address answering, and writes that wait in the connection pooler at the switch instead of failing.

New PostgreSQL installs from the catalog come with a connection pooler. `FLUI_CONNECTION_URL` goes through it; `FLUI_DIRECT_URL` goes straight to the database for schema migrations, LISTEN and admin tools. Existing installs are unchanged.
See who is connected to a managed PostgreSQL, who blocks whom and what each session runs, then cancel a query or close a session, from the Sessions tab, `flui db sessions` or an agent.
The installation can run its own image registry, on a disk or on a bucket, with credentials per application and measured space and traffic.
The API can run as several copies; a cluster's public names follow the nodes that take traffic, and an application says whether it survives losing a worker.
Application and cluster pages show peaks, throttling and health checks, with alerts on bandwidth, surges and edge errors that link to the page that explains them.
This release needs the new bootstrap: install or upgrade it with the CLI.

Every backup is encrypted at rest with keys Flui already holds, and application volumes are backed up as deduplicated snapshots per application: browse a backup, restore one file or the whole volume, from the CLI, MCP or dashboard.
Protect a whole cluster in one step: every application, new ones included, gets the backup that fits it, and databases Flui cannot copy consistently are listed for a decision.

A rebuild brings volumes back from their snapshots and applications back in dependency order; after a platform restore, `flui cluster rebuild-control` brings back the applications that ran on the control cluster.
Velero is no longer used. Run `flui backup velero uninstall <cluster>` where it is installed; its old backups stay in the bucket and the command lists the folders to remove.
Restoring an encrypted PostgreSQL backup, and compressed MariaDB backups, need the database images published with this release; new databases and restores pull them.
The sign-in relay moves to flui-authz 0.7.0, which asks the API instead of checking tokens itself.

An update no longer risks stopping the platform database on an installation built before 0.13.0-rc.9. The update would have replaced the database and cache manifests with ones that run at the platform priority while leaving out the file that creates that priority, so their pods could not start again. The file now comes with them, and an update holds back any manifest whose priority it does not bring.

Coming from 0.13.0-rc.8: that release cannot run this update itself — its updater stops at the first step, before changing anything. Move the API and the dashboard to 0.13.0-rc.10 first; from there `flui env upgrade` brings the manifests forward.

Includes everything in 0.13.0-rc.9: one planned update for the whole installation (`flui env upgrade`), access granted for a limited time, the activity record, and alert destinations by email and signed webhook.

New: one planned update for the whole installation. `flui env upgrade`, or Updates in the dashboard, shows the plan — back up the platform, bring every cluster's system manifests forward, roll out the platform components, upgrade K3s one minor version at a time with workload clusters before the control cluster, then check the result — and changes nothing until you confirm it.

Coming from 0.13.0-rc.8: that release cannot run this update itself — its updater stops at the first step, before changing anything. Move the API and the dashboard to 0.13.0-rc.9 first; from there `flui env upgrade` brings the manifests forward.
A new control cluster installs again. The installer pinned by 0.13.0-rc.8 stopped at the first system manifest that declares no values.

Access can be given for a limited time: `flui iam grant add --expires`, or Access → Temporary access in the dashboard. It lapses on its own, and administrators are told when it is given, the day before it ends and when it ends. The new platform_operator role runs clusters, nodes, updates and backups without reaching any application data.
Every change, every refused request and every read of application data is recorded: `flui audit list`, or Access → Activity in the dashboard.

Alerts reach people outside the dashboard: email and signed webhook destinations, for infrastructure alerts or for everything (`flui alerts destination add`). New alerts fire when a backup fails and when a certificate is not renewed in time.

Every alert now names the application it is about. The installer was blanking the label references in every alert annotation, so a firing alert said "Application  is down" with nothing in the gap. New nodes get the fix from the bootstrap; an installation already standing repairs it with `flui env refresh-manifests`.

Applications in the demo sandbox are reachable again. A guest's area fenced out the ingress controller itself, so anything a guest deployed answered 502 and never obtained a certificate. Existing guest areas keep the old rule and have to be recycled.
An application's address now appears on its own once the certificate is issued, instead of waiting for somebody to open the networking screens.
The state Flui shows for an application is re-read every five minutes. It was the outcome of the last deploy, frozen — so a pod that died an hour later still read as running.
A workload refused by the cluster now says why within seconds, instead of timing out after five minutes with no cause. The same reason is now carried on a cluster that failed to delete.

Every container has a ceiling on what it may write outside its volumes, set on the namespace and overridable per application. Nothing outside the demo sandbox had one, and what fills is the node's own disk.
Installing from the catalog keeps the name you chose, and a restart of the API mid-install no longer leaves two copies of the application.

New: `flui env refresh-manifests` brings the manifests a cluster restarts from into line with a release. It shows what would change and writes nothing unless asked, never touches a file holding a secret, and supplies no values.

Every node now gets a quota-capable filesystem for application data, so a tenancy's disk ceiling can be enforced and one workload can no longer fill the node's root disk. New nodes only: a bootstrap script runs when a node is created.
A guest's enforced disk ceiling is now sized for the bytes they write, separately from the declared sizes that govern how many applications they may install.
The CLI names a locked vault instead of reporting a decryption failure, and says when a health check could not reach the cluster rather than calling every service down.
Node-local storage is a quota-capable filesystem of its own, so a tenancy's disk ceiling can be enforced and one workload can no longer fill the node's root disk.
Storage usage is measured per application and per tenancy, and a volume can be resized where the storage class allows it.
Critical alerts reach the instance's administrators by email, including the ones no application owns.
Guest inference is metered and pinned to the model the instance chose.
Deploy from a repository: Flui reads it, renders its manifests, and applies them on a branch of its own
Backups: continuous protection with point-in-time restore, scheduled volume copies, and retention
Rebuild a lost cluster from its sealed bundle, and put the data back where the ledger says
Apply a Flui release from the running installation
Cluster rebuild — recover a lost cluster from its last backup without recreating apps by hand.
Backup quick setup — one command wires a destination, a policy and the first job.
MariaDB point-in-time restore joins the Postgres continuous-backup engine.
Server adoption checks ownership before applying firewall rules.
